nuance.usage_note: Americans use egoism mostly in philosophy classes, ethics debates, or formal writing about character. In everyday speech, people say 'selfishness' or 'self-interest'. Be careful: egoism can mean a moral theory, while egotism means excessive talk about oneself.

distinctions.note: Egotism means talking too much about yourself or boasting, while egoism means putting your own interests first in action or morality.
Selfishness is the everyday word for refusing to share or help, while egoism is a more formal term, often used for a theory or principle.

examples.everyday: That kind of egoism is why he never helps with the dishes.
examples.professional: Her approach to negotiating is pure egoism, so she rarely considers the other side's interests.
examples.analytical: Ethical egoism claims that acting for one's own benefit is the only rational basis for morality, a position many critics find hard to defend.

nuance.analogy: Egoism is like a compass that points only to your own interests, ignoring the road others are traveling.
nuance.etymology: From Latin ego, I, plus the suffix -ism.
common_mistakes: Using egoism to mean talking about oneself too much; that meaning belongs to egotism.
Pronouncing the first syllable as 'eg' instead of 'EE'.

egoism.etymology: From French *égoïsme*, from New Latin *egoismus*, from Latin *ego*.

senses.definition: An advocate of egoism.
An egocentric or self-centered person.
An egotist (a person who talks excessively about themselves).
senses.example: My brother is such an egoist that every conversation somehow turns back to his own achievements.

core.definition: A self-centered person who puts their own interests first; also a person who holds egoism, the philosophical view that self-interest is the basis of morality.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, EE. Say the second syllable as 'goh' with a clear long o, and do not reduce it to a schwa. The final -ist is a short 'ist'.

nuance.connotation: Negative in everyday use, meaning someone selfish; neutral when used as a term in philosophy to name a position.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, calling someone an egoist is a criticism of selfishness, though people more often say selfish or self-centered. In philosophy classes and writing, egoist names someone who holds ethical egoism. Americans usually say egotist for someone who boasts about themselves, so the two words are often confused.

distinctions.note: An egoist acts for their own benefit at others' expense; an egotist talks excessively about themselves and their achievements.
Selfish is an everyday word for lacking concern for others; egoist is more formal and can also name a philosophical position.

examples.everyday: Don't invite Mark to the team lunch if you want to split the bill; he's a total egoist about money.
examples.professional: We need to hire people who think about the whole team, not someone who acts like an egoist and takes all the credit.
examples.analytical: Ethical egoism is often criticized because the egoist's claim that everyone should pursue self-interest seems to undermine the cooperation that moral life requires.

nuance.analogy: An egoist is like a person who always takes the biggest slice of the cake and then argues that everyone else should do the same.
nuance.etymology: From French égoïste, from Latin ego, meaning 'I'.
common_mistakes: Using egoist to mean someone who only talks about themselves; that meaning belongs to egotist.
Pronouncing the middle as 'ego' with a short e instead of the long EE in the first syllable.

senses.definition: Originally, a property of amber and certain other nonconducting substances to attract lightweight material when rubbed, or the cause of this property; now understood to be a phenomenon caused by the distribution and movement of charged subatomic particles and their interaction with the electromagnetic field.
A feeling of excitement; a thrill.
senses.example: Opening night for the new production had an electricity unlike other openings.

senses.definition: Electrical power, as supplied by power stations or generators.
senses.example: This heater draws more than a thousand watts of electricity.

senses.definition: Electrical energy, as supplied by power stations or generators.
senses.example: Last year this portion of the grid consumed more than a thousand megawatt-hours of electricity.

senses.definition: The supply of electricity, as a utility.
senses.example: Electricity bosses set to make record profits.

senses.definition: The study of electrical phenomena; the branch of science dealing with such phenomena.
senses.example: He took up the job of studying electricity in college.

core.definition: The power supplied through wires to run lights, appliances, and machines in homes and businesses.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on tris, and the second syllable -ic- is pronounced as an s sound, not a k sound. The final -ity is a reduced ih-tee, and the vowel in the first syllable is short.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in everyday use; in physics, the term refers to a natural phenomenon.
nuance.usage_note: In American conversation, electricity usually means the power supply in a house or building, as in the electricity went out or the electricity bill. The word is uncountable, so Americans do not say an electricity. In figurative use, electricity can also mean a thrill or charged atmosphere.

distinctions.note: Power in everyday speech can mean the electricity supply, but in physics power is the rate of energy transfer.
Energy is a broad term for the capacity to do work, while electricity is one specific form of energy that flows through wires.

examples.everyday: The electricity went out during the storm, so we ate dinner by candlelight.
examples.professional: Our data center's electricity costs doubled this year, so we're moving some workloads to a cheaper region.
examples.analytical: Electricity, once known only as a curious property of amber, now grounds the physics of the electromagnetic field.

nuance.analogy: Electricity is like water moving through pipes, except the pipes are wires and the water is electric charge.
nuance.etymology: From New Latin electricitas, from Latin electrum, amber, from Greek elektron.
common_mistakes: Saying an electricity or electricities, since the everyday sense is uncountable.
Stressing the first syllable as EL-ek-tri-city instead of ih-lek-TRIS-ih-tee.

senses.definition: Relating to the basic, essential or fundamental part of something.
senses.example: Learning the elementary rules of grammar is essential before writing a research paper.

senses.definition: Very simple.
Relating to an elementary school.
senses.example: My daughter starts elementary school next fall, so we're visiting the campus this week.

senses.definition: Fundamental: serving as a building block for more complicated structures or processes.
senses.example: Arrays are elementary structures that most programs use to store ordered data.

senses.definition: Which performs a row or column operation on another matrix when the two are multiplied; see Elementary matrix on Wikipedia.Wikipedia (Such matrices are called "elementary" because they generate the general linear group).
senses.example: Multiplying by an elementary matrix swaps two rows, which is a useful step in Gaussian elimination.

senses.definition: Arising from Vieta's formulas; see Elementary symmetric polynomial on Wikipedia.Wikipedia.
senses.example: Vieta's formulas express each coefficient as an elementary symmetric polynomial of the roots.

senses.definition: Straightforward, employing only basic techniques; not requiring substantial knowledge (of some particular domain, object, etc.).
senses.example: The puzzle looked elementary, but the hidden trap in the last step caught everyone.

senses.definition: Relating to a subatomic particle.
senses.example: Physicists classify the electron as an elementary particle with no known internal structure.

senses.definition: Involving only a single reaction step and transition state.
senses.example: This elementary reaction happens in one step, with a single transition state between reactants and products.

senses.definition: Making no use of complex analysis.
senses.example: The proof is elementary, using only algebra and no complex analysis at all.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of elementary school.
senses.example: At Lakeside Elementary I learned to appreciate the forest.

senses.definition: A supernatural being associated with the elements.
senses.example: In the old tale, an elementary rose from the lake to warn the village of the flood.

core.definition: Very basic or simple, dealing only with the fundamental parts of a subject or task.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on MEN, and the vowels before and after it are reduced, so say 'el-uh-men-tuh-ree' without an extra 'ay' sound in the middle. The final syllable is a short 'ee', not 'air-ee', and the r is pronounced in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when it means basic, but it can sound condescending when used for someone's knowledge ('That's elementary') and is positive in 'elementary school' and 'elementary principles'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'elementary school' for grades K through 5 and use 'elementary' alone to mean very simple or basic. Saying 'That's elementary' can sound dismissive, so use it carefully in conversation. For a simple task, Americans more often say 'easy' or 'simple'.

distinctions.note: Basic is neutral and common in everyday speech, while elementary suggests a level so simple it may seem too easy or too early in learning.
Simple describes something uncomplicated, but elementary also implies a fundamental level or a lack of advanced knowledge.

examples.everyday: Fixing a running toilet is pretty elementary once you know where the shutoff valve is.
examples.professional: The elementary version of the model uses just one feature, so we can start there before adding the others.
examples.analytical: The argument rests on an elementary distinction between appearance and reality that the critic never fully defends.

nuance.analogy: Like the foundation of a house, the elementary level is the first layer everything else rests on.
nuance.etymology: From Latin elementarius, relating to the elements or first principles, from elementum.
common_mistakes: Using 'elementary' for a primary school in the US; the usual term is 'elementary school', and 'primary school' is more British.
Saying 'elementary' with stress on the final syllable, as in 'el-uh-men-TAIR-ee'.
Confusing 'elementary' with 'elemental', which means basic or related to natural forces.

elementary.etymology: From Middle English *elementare*, from Latin *elementārius* (“elementary”), from *elementum* (“one of the four elements of antiquity; fundamentals”) + *-ārius*.

senses.definition: To evoke, educe (emotions, feelings, responses, etc.); to generate, obtain, or provoke as a response or answer.
To draw out, bring out, bring forth (something latent); to obtain information from someone or something.
senses.example: Fred wished to elicit the time of the meeting from Jane.

senses.definition: To use logic to arrive at truth; to derive by reason.

core.definition: To draw out or bring forth a response, reaction, information or feeling from someone, often with effort or skill.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, LIS. The final 't' is a light, unreleased sound, and the middle vowel is a short 'i'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes drawing out a reaction, which can be positive or negative depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use elicit mostly in professional, legal, academic and journalistic writing, and in meetings when discussing feedback or responses. In casual speech, people more often say get or bring out. Note that elicit is a verb, not an adjective.

distinctions.note: Illicit means illegal or forbidden; it is a false friend with a similar sound.
Evoke often describes a feeling or memory arising by itself, while elicit implies deliberate effort to produce a response.
Extract means to pull something out, often by force; elicit usually means drawing out information or reaction through questions or stimuli.

examples.everyday: My friend's joke didn't elicit a single laugh at the party.
examples.professional: Our user interviews were designed to elicit honest feedback about the new dashboard.
examples.analytical: The philosopher's question was intended to elicit a clearer statement of the premise.

nuance.analogy: Like a fishing line that draws a fish up from deep water.
nuance.etymology: From Latin elicere, to draw out, from e- (out) and lacere (to entice).
common_mistakes: Confusing elicit with illicit, which means illegal.
Using elicit as an adjective or as a synonym for 'explicit'.

senses.definition: To completely remove, get rid of, put an end to.
To kill (a person or animal).
senses.example: a ruthless mobster who eliminated his enemies

senses.definition: To exclude (from investigation or from further competition).
senses.example: Bill was eliminated as a suspect when the police interviewed witnesses.

senses.definition: To record amounts in a consolidation statement to remove the effects of inter-company transactions.
senses.example: The accountants will eliminate intercompany sales from the consolidated statements before reporting group revenue.

senses.definition: To render (a facility) unusable, to destroy it; to disable (a soldier), make them unable to fight (typically but not necessarily by killing)
senses.example: The bombers were sent to eliminate the enemy's fuel depot and its pumping station.

senses.definition: To excrete (waste products).
senses.example: The kidneys eliminate waste products from the blood and send them out as urine.

core.definition: To remove or get rid of something completely, or to rule someone or something out of consideration or a competition.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LIM, the second syllable. The middle vowels reduce to 'ih', so avoid saying 'ee-LIM-in-ate' with a long vowel in each syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses, such as eliminating waste or options; it can sound harsh or clinical when it refers to people, and in news about violence it is blunt.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use eliminate all the time for removing problems, options, costs, or habits, as in 'eliminate sugar' or 'eliminate the middleman'. In sports, a team is eliminated when it loses out of a tournament. For killing a person, news writers may say eliminate, but in everyday talk people say kill or take out, so use eliminate carefully.

distinctions.note: Reduce means to make something smaller or less, while eliminate means to remove it completely.
Exclude means to leave something or someone out, while eliminate often means removing something entirely, sometimes after a process of testing or competition.
Kill means to cause death directly, while eliminate is broader and can be used for removing things or, in clinical or news language, for people.

examples.everyday: If we cut the coffee and the sugar, that should eliminate most of my afternoon crashes.
examples.professional: We can eliminate the duplicate records by matching on email address before we load the table.
examples.analytical: The argument is that a single counterexample is enough to eliminate the universal claim, though it may leave a weaker version standing.

nuance.analogy: Like pulling a weed out by the root so it cannot grow back, to eliminate something means to remove it completely.
nuance.etymology: From Latin eliminare, 'to drive out, remove', from e- 'out' and limen 'threshold'.
common_mistakes: Using eliminate to mean reduce when something remains; eliminate means removed completely.
Writing eliminate of instead of eliminate from or using it with a direct object, as in eliminate the candidate.

eliminate.etymology: Latin *ēlīminātus*, perfect passive participle of *ēlīminō* (“to turn out of doors, banish”), from *ex-* + *līmen* + *-ō* (see *-ate*), akin to; see also and *limen*.

senses.definition: A surface, all of whose cross sections are elliptic or circular (including the sphere), that generalises the ellipse and in Cartesian coordinates (x, y, z) is a quadric with equation x/a + y/b + z/c = 1.
senses.example: The engineers modeled the Earth as an ellipsoid to calculate distances more accurately.

senses.definition: Such a surface used as a model of the shape of the earth.
senses.example: Here the geoid is thirty meters below the ellipsoid.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to an ellipse; elliptic.
senses.example: The ellipsoid curve on the graph represented the relationship between the two variables.

senses.definition: Shaped like an ellipse; elliptical.
senses.example: The ellipsoid pebble had been worn smooth by centuries of river water.

senses.definition: Having the tridimensional shape of an ellipse rotated on its long axis.
senses.example: The lens was ellipsoid, like a flattened egg spun around its long axis.

core.definition: Noun: a three-dimensional surface shaped like a stretched sphere, used to model objects like the Earth. Adjective: shaped like an ellipsoid.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, LIP. The final syllable rhymes with void, so the ending sounds like -soyd. Avoid pronouncing it as -sode.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term in mathematics, geodesy, and engineering.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ellipsoid mostly in technical settings such as geodesy, GPS, cartography, and 3D modeling. In casual talk, people would say egg-shaped or stretched ball. In professional contexts, the reference ellipsoid of the Earth is a standard term.

distinctions.note: A sphere has equal radii in all directions. An ellipsoid is stretched or compressed along one or more axes.
An ellipse is two-dimensional. An ellipsoid is the three-dimensional counterpart.

examples.everyday: The globe on my desk is a sphere, but the real Earth is more like a slightly squashed ellipsoid.
examples.professional: The GPS software uses a reference ellipsoid to convert the satellite coordinates into latitude and longitude.
examples.analytical: Approximating the Earth as a perfect sphere simplifies the calculation, yet the oblate ellipsoid captures the flattening at the poles that affects precise measurement.

nuance.analogy: An ellipsoid is like a sphere that has been gently pressed at the top and bottom, like a squashed ball.
nuance.etymology: From ellipse plus -oid, meaning resembling.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the ending as -soid, rhyming with void instead of void-like sound -soyd.
Using ellipsoid to mean any irregular blob; it must have a precise elliptical cross-section.

senses.definition: To steal or misappropriate money that one has been trusted with, especially to steal money from the organization for which one works.
senses.example: The bookkeeper was arrested after she embezzled nearly two hundred thousand dollars from the church.

core.definition: To secretly steal money or property that you were trusted to manage, usually from the organization you work for.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, BEZ, and the final syllable is a light, reduced 'uhl', not 'ell'. Don't say 'em-bez-ZULL' or add an extra vowel after the z.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It always implies a serious crime, usually a betrayal of trust by someone in a position of responsibility.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use embezzle mainly for financial crimes by employees, treasurers, accountants or board members, and it often appears in news reports and court cases. In everyday talk people more often say 'stole money from the company' or 'ripped off the church'. The related crime is 'embezzlement', and the person is an 'embezzler'.

distinctions.note: Steal is the general word for taking anything that belongs to someone else. Embezzle is narrower: it means taking money or property you were trusted to look after.
Fraud is a broader legal category of deceiving someone for gain. Embezzlement is a specific kind of theft by a trusted person.

examples.everyday: My neighbor's brother got arrested because he embezzled money from the church where he was treasurer.
examples.professional: The internal audit found that a senior accountant had embezzled about forty thousand dollars from vendor payments over two years.
examples.analytical: Embezzlement differs from ordinary theft because the offender first gains lawful control of the property and then misappropriates it through a breach of trust.

nuance.analogy: Embezzling is like a house sitter who quietly takes the valuables they were hired to protect.
nuance.etymology: From Anglo-Norman embesiler, to make away with property; the deeper origin is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Using 'embezzle' for any kind of theft, such as shoplifting, which is simply 'steal'.
Spelling it with two z's or with an 's' in the middle; the American spelling is 'embezzle' with one z before the final e sound.

embezzle.etymology: From Middle English *embesilen*, from Anglo-Norman *embesiler*, *embesillier*, *embeseillier* (“to steal, cause to disappear”), from *em-* + Old French *besillier* (“to torment, destroy, gouge”), of unknown origin.

senses.definition: A representative symbol, such as a trademark, a badge or logo.
senses.example: The medical trucks were emblazoned with the emblem of the Red Cross.

senses.definition: Something that represents a larger whole.
senses.example: The rampant poverty in the ethnic slums was just an emblem of the group's disenfranchisement by the society as a whole.

senses.definition: Inlay; inlaid or mosaic work; something ornamental inserted in a surface.
senses.example: The jewelry box had a mosaic emblem of gold and mother-of-pearl inlaid in its lid.

senses.definition: A picture accompanied with a motto, a set of verses, etc. intended as a moral lesson or meditation.
senses.example: The old book of emblems paired each woodcut with a verse about patience and faith.

senses.definition: A picture placed on the field of the escutcheon.
senses.example: The family's crest showed a silver emblem on the shield, a lion rampant.

core.definition: A visual symbol that represents a group, idea, or organization, such as a logo, badge, or trademark.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The second syllable is a reduced vowel, so don't say 'em-BLAY-um'; the final 'm' is a clear, short closure.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests something meaningful and recognizable, and it is often used for logos and national or religious symbols.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'emblem' for logos, badges, and symbols that stand for something larger, like a national flag or a team crest. In everyday talk people more often say 'logo' for company marks and 'symbol' for general representation. 'Emblem' sounds slightly more traditional and dignified.

distinctions.note: A logo is a company's graphic mark; an emblem can be any representative symbol, including a crest or badge.
'Symbol' is the broader and more common word; 'emblem' suggests a more fixed, official, or heraldic image.

collocations: the emblem of a sports team
a badge of honor and emblem

examples.everyday: That bald eagle on the jacket is the emblem of our high school team.
examples.professional: We redesigned the emblem for the product launch, so the new logo should appear on every slide and email template.
examples.analytical: In the Christian tradition the cross serves as an emblem of redemption, condensing a whole story of suffering and hope into a single image.

nuance.analogy: An emblem is like a flag in a single stitch: a small image that carries the whole identity of a group.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'emblema,' from Greek 'emblēma,' meaning 'something inserted or inlaid,' from 'emballein,' 'to throw in.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (em-BLEM); the stress is on the first syllable.
Confusing 'emblem' with 'emblematic' as a noun; 'emblematic' is an adjective, so say 'an emblematic building', not 'an emblematic'.

emblem.etymology: From Old French *embleme*, from Latin *emblēma* (“raised ornaments on vessels, tessellated work, mosaic”), from Ancient Greek *ἔμβλημα* (“an insertion”), from *ἐμβάλλειν* (“to put in, to lay on”).

senses.definition: Embryonic.

core.definition: Of or relating to an embryo, or to very early undeveloped tissue; the medical term used mainly in phrases such as embryonal tumor.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, BRY, which differs from embryonic, where the stress falls on the -ON syllable. Keep the final syllable short and reduced, like 'nul'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and clinical.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use embryonal mainly in pathology and oncology, in terms such as embryonal carcinoma. For general description of early development, Americans normally say embryonic instead.

distinctions.note: Embryonic is the general adjective for anything at an early stage of development; embryonal is mainly limited to medical terms about tissues or tumors.

examples.everyday: My doctor said the lump was an embryonal tumor, which means it grew from very early tissue.
examples.professional: The pathology report classified the lesion as embryonal carcinoma, so the oncology team scheduled chemotherapy.
examples.analytical: Embryonal cells retain pluripotency, a capacity that distinguishes them from fully differentiated adult tissue.

nuance.analogy: Embryonal tissue is like an unfinished blueprint: every possible part of the building is still represented, but none has been fixed in place.
nuance.etymology: From embryo and the adjective suffix -al.
common_mistakes: Using embryonal in everyday speech where embryonic is the normal word.
Shifting the stress to the first syllable (EM-bry-nul).

senses.definition: A non-wage compensation provided to an employee in addition to his normal wage or salary.

core.definition: A non-wage perk, such as health insurance or retirement contributions, that an employer provides in addition to pay.

pronunciation.tip: There are two main stresses: the last syllable of employee (EE) and the first syllable of benefit (BEN). Benefit is often reduced to BEN-uh-fit, with the middle vowel almost silent.

nuance.connotation: Positive from the employee's side; the term is neutral in HR and business, and benefits can be a key factor in job decisions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans discuss benefits constantly when comparing job offers, during open enrollment and in HR emails. The phrase 'benefits package' is standard, and 'the benefits' alone usually means health insurance and retirement plans. Casually, people may just say 'perks'.

distinctions.note: Salary is the regular cash pay an employee receives; benefits are non-cash items added on top of it.
Perk is informal and can mean any extra, like free coffee; employee benefit usually refers to formal programs such as insurance or retirement plans.

examples.everyday: The best part of the new job is the employee benefits, especially the dental plan.
examples.professional: Please review the employee benefit changes in the email from HR before open enrollment closes.
examples.analytical: Employee benefits such as health coverage tie workers to their employers, which some economists argue reduces labor mobility.

nuance.analogy: Employee benefits are like the free toppings on a pizza: the base price is the salary, but the extras add real value.
nuance.etymology: Employee comes from employ; benefit comes from Old French bienfait, from Latin benefactum, 'well done'.
common_mistakes: Treating benefits as a single cash payment; they are usually non-cash and are counted separately from salary.
Using 'a benefit package' and 'benefits' interchangeably without noticing that 'benefits' alone usually means insurance and retirement.

senses.definition: The act of encouraging.
senses.example: Her steady encouragement helped me finish the marathon training program.

senses.definition: Something that incites, supports, promotes, protects or advances; incentive.
senses.example: Free tuition was a strong encouragement for students to pursue nursing degrees.

senses.definition: Words or actions that increase someone's confidence.
The feeling of being encouraged.
senses.example: Her teacher's kind words gave him a surge of encouragement before the exam.

core.definition: Words or actions that increase someone's confidence, hope, or motivation to keep going.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, KUR, and the vowel is a relaxed 'uh' sound with a strong American r. Don't pronounce the final 't' too sharply; it is light, and the 'j' sound in the middle is soft.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes support that makes someone feel more capable or hopeful. It can also be used in a more abstract sense, such as an 'encouragement' to do something, which is a bit more formal.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use encouragement often in everyday speech, at work, and at church, usually as a mass noun: 'She needs encouragement.' A natural reply to a thank-you is 'Anytime' or 'I'm glad it helped.' In casual speech, people more often say 'a little encouragement' or 'a bit of encouragement' than 'many encouragements.'

distinctions.note: Support is broader and can mean practical help or money, while encouragement is specifically about boosting someone's confidence or spirit.
Praise is an evaluation of something done well; encouragement looks forward and motivates someone to keep trying.

examples.everyday: Thanks for the encouragement before my job interview; it really helped me relax.
examples.professional: Your manager's encouragement about the new project should give you confidence to propose your own ideas.
examples.analytical: Scripture often presents encouragement as a communal duty, not merely a private feeling of comfort.

nuance.analogy: Encouragement is like a tailwind for a runner: it doesn't run the race for you, but it makes the next steps feel easier.
nuance.etymology: From encourage plus the suffix -ment, from Old French encouragier, to hearten.
common_mistakes: Using 'encouragements' as a plural in everyday speech; the noun is usually uncountable.
Pronouncing the stress on the first syllable (EN-cour-age-ment) instead of the second.

senses.definition: The quality of being an enemy; a hostile or unfriendly disposition.
A state or feeling of opposition, hostility, hatred or animosity.
1 2 3 “enmity” listed in the Oxford English Dictionary [2 Ed. 1989]

core.definition: Deep hostility or hatred between people or groups; a long-standing feeling of opposition or ill will.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, EN. The last two syllables are weak, so the middle vowel is a quick 'ih' and the ending is a light 'tee'.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. It implies a serious and lasting hostility, not a passing argument.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'enmity' in writing, history, politics and religious contexts to describe deep, long-term hostility. In casual speech they say 'bad blood,' 'hard feelings' or 'they can't stand each other.' Using it for a minor disagreement sounds exaggerated.

distinctions.note: Hostility is open aggression or unfriendliness in the moment; enmity implies a deeper, more lasting hatred.
Animosity is a strong dislike, often emotional; enmity is more formal and suggests an enduring state of opposition.

examples.everyday: The two neighbors have had real enmity for years, ever since the fence dispute.
examples.professional: Years of enmity between the two departments made it hard to agree on a shared data standard.
examples.analytical: Augustine traces human enmity back to the disordered love that turns people against one another and against God.

nuance.analogy: Enmity is like a root under a house: hidden, deep and hard to pull out even when the surface looks calm.
nuance.etymology: From Old French 'enemistié,' from 'enemi' (enemy), from Latin 'inimicus' (unfriendly, hostile).
common_mistakes: Using 'enmity' for a small disagreement; it describes something much stronger.
Writing 'enmity' with the stress on the wrong syllable, as in 'en-MIH-tee.'

enmity.etymology: From Middle English *enemyte*, from Old French *enemisté*, *ennemistié*, from Late Latin, Vulgar Latin **inimīcitās*, from Latin *inimīcus* (“enemy”).

senses.definition: The state of being noble.
The act of ennobling or something which ennobles.
senses.example: Her grandfather saw the volunteer work as an ennoblement of ordinary lives.

core.definition: The act of raising someone to a noble rank or the process of giving dignity, honor or moral worth.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, NOH. Say the middle 'bul' quickly and let the final 'ment' be weak and short.

nuance.connotation: Positive in most contexts, but it can be neutral when describing a formal title or honor.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'ennoblement' mostly in historical, academic or literary writing, such as discussions of medieval titles or moral philosophy. In daily talk it is almost never used. People would say 'raising to the peerage' for British titles or 'becoming a noble' in general.

distinctions.note: Ennoble is the verb for the action; ennoblement is the noun for the process or result.
Elevation is a general word for raising in rank or quality; ennoblement specifically implies noble status or moral dignity.

examples.everyday: The old story about the family's ennoblement is a little hard to believe.
examples.professional: The report traced the ennoblement of several industrialists in the nineteenth century.
examples.analytical: Nietzsche's critique of ennoblement questions whether moral dignity is really conferred from outside or cultivated from within.

nuance.analogy: Ennoblement is like a title deed to a higher status, recorded and officially given.
nuance.etymology: From 'ennoble' plus the suffix '-ment,' from Old French 'ennobler' and Latin 'nobilis.'
common_mistakes: Using 'ennoblement' in everyday speech where 'honor' or 'promotion' is more natural.
Mixing up the noun and the verb; say 'the ennoblement of a family' but 'to ennoble a family.'

senses.definition: To occur afterwards, as a result or effect.
senses.example: Give three freshmen six bottles of wine, and hilarity will ensue.

core.definition: To happen afterward as a result or consequence of something, often used for a chain of events or an outcome.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, -SOO. The first syllable is a short, reduced in, so the word sounds like in-SOO, not en-SOO.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes sequence and consequence without judging whether the result is good or bad.
nuance.usage_note: Ensue is common in American news, reports, and formal writing, as in confusion ensued or a debate ensued. In casual speech Americans more often say happen next, follow, or result. It can sound stiff in a relaxed conversation, so use it when describing a sequence of events in writing or in a formal presentation.

distinctions.note: Follow is simpler and neutral, while ensue suggests a more formal or dramatic consequence that comes after a notable event.
Result emphasizes cause and effect, while ensue emphasizes what comes afterward in time.

examples.everyday: The power went out during the game, and a loud argument ensued between the fans in the stands.
examples.professional: After the server migration failed, a long outage ensued, and the team spent the weekend restoring data.
examples.analytical: When the treaty collapsed, a decade of instability ensued, and historians still debate which decisions caused it.

nuance.analogy: Ensue is like a stone dropped into a pond: the ripples that follow are the consequences, spreading out after the first moment.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English ensuen, from Old French ensuivre, from Latin insequi, to follow after.
common_mistakes: Saying ensue to mean ensure; these are different words with different meanings.
Using ensue for a result that is planned, when it is better to say result in or lead to.

ensue.etymology: From Old French ensu, stem of some conjugated forms of *ensuivre* (“follow close upon, come afterward”) (French *ensuivre*); see *sequel*.

senses.definition: A measure of the amount of energy in a physical system that cannot be used to do work.
senses.example: The compression algorithm works by reducing the entropy of the signal, removing redundant bits.

senses.definition: A measure of the amount of information and noise present in a signal.
senses.example: The compression algorithm works by reducing the entropy of the signal, removing redundant bits.

senses.definition: A measure of the disorder present in a system.
A measure of the disorder directly proportional to the natural logarithm of the number of microstates yielding an equivalent thermodynamic macrostate.
senses.example: Boltzmann's formula links entropy to the logarithm of the number of microstates compatible with a macrostate.

senses.definition: Shannon entropy.
senses.example: We calculated the Shannon entropy of each column to rank the features by information content.

senses.definition: The capacity factor for thermal energy that is hidden with respect to temperature.
senses.example: The chemist measured how the crystal's entropy changed as the sample warmed from near absolute zero.

senses.definition: The dispersal of energy; how much energy is spread out in a process, or how widely spread out it becomes, at a specific temperature.
senses.example: As the gas expands into the empty chamber, its energy spreads out and entropy grows.

senses.definition: The tendency of a system that is left to itself to descend into chaos.
senses.example: Left alone, every messy system tends toward entropy, and my garage is proof.

core.definition: A measure of disorder in a system; in information theory, the average uncertainty or information contained in a message.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle syllable is a reduced 'ruh,' and the final syllable is a clear 'ee.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral in technical use; in casual speech it can carry a sense of gradual decline or decay.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use entropy precisely in physics, information theory, and data science, and loosely in everyday talk to mean gradual decline, as in the entropy of a messy house. In meetings, be ready to define it, since listeners may mean different things.

distinctions.note: Disorder is an everyday word for messiness; entropy is a precise quantity with exact mathematical definitions.
Information measures how much uncertainty is reduced by a message; entropy measures the average uncertainty before the outcome is known.

examples.everyday: My kitchen drawers always lose their order, a little entropy every week.
examples.professional: Our cross-entropy loss dropped steadily across training epochs, so the classifier is getting more confident.
examples.analytical: Boltzmann's statistical account links entropy to the number of microscopic arrangements compatible with a given macrostate.

nuance.analogy: Entropy is like a deck of cards: a freshly sorted deck is low in entropy, and every shuffle pushes it toward a more mixed state.
nuance.etymology: Coined by Rudolf Clausius in 1865 from Greek en- plus tropē, meaning transformation.
common_mistakes: Using entropy as a synonym for chaos in technical writing, where it has a precise definition.
Stressing the second syllable as en-TROH-pee instead of EN-truh-pee.

senses.definition: Upright; vertical or reaching broadly upwards.
senses.example: The flagpole stood erect in the center of the empty courtyard.

senses.definition: Rigid, firm; standing out perpendicularly, especially as the result of stimulation.
senses.example: The penis should be fully erect before commencing copulation.

senses.definition: Having an erect penis or clitoris.
senses.example: OK, baby, I'm erect now. Let's get it on!

senses.definition: Watchful; alert.
senses.example: The sentry stood erect at the gate, scanning the road for visitors.

senses.definition: Elevated, as the tips of wings, heads of serpents, etc.
senses.example: The heron stood in the shallows, its feathers erect against the wind.

senses.definition: To put up by the fitting together of materials or parts.
senses.example: to erect a house or a fort

senses.definition: To cause to stand up or out.
senses.example: The crew erected a tall tent before the storm reached the valley.

senses.definition: To raise and place in an upright or perpendicular position; to set upright; to raise.
senses.example: to erect a pole, a flagstaff, a monument, etc.

senses.definition: To spin up and align to vertical.
senses.example: As soon as electrical power was restored, the attitude indicators' gyros would have begun to erect.

senses.definition: To lift up; to elevate; to exalt; to magnify.
senses.example: The sermon sought to erect Christ's mercy above all human judgment.

senses.definition: To animate; to encourage; to cheer.
senses.example: Her words erected my spirits when I felt like giving up.

senses.definition: To cast or draw up (a figure of the heavens, horoscope etc.).
senses.example: The astronomer erected a horoscope for the child born under that autumn moon.

senses.definition: To enter a state of physiological erection.
senses.example: Some medications can make it harder for men to erect.

senses.definition: To set up as an assertion or consequence from premises, etc.
senses.example: From these premises the logician erected a conclusion that followed necessarily.

senses.definition: To set up or establish; to found; to form; to institute.
senses.example: The city council erected a new library on the site of the old mill.

core.definition: Standing straight up and upright, or built and set in an upright position.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable. The 'r' is clearly rhotic, and the vowel is a short 'eh,' not 'ay.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes posture or position; in some contexts it can refer to anatomy, which is not the sense learners need first.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'erect' as an adjective for posture, such as 'stand erect,' and as a verb for building, such as 'erect a barrier.' In everyday talk, people more often say 'upright' or 'straight' for posture and 'build' or 'put up' for structures. Avoid using 'erect' casually to describe people's bodies, since it can sound clinical.

distinctions.note: 'Upright' is everyday and neutral; 'erect' is more formal and can imply a deliberate, stiff posture.
'Build' is the everyday verb for construction; 'erect' is more formal and often used for temporary or large structures like tents or fences.

examples.everyday: The camp counselor told us to stand erect while we waited for the bus.
examples.professional: Crews will erect a temporary fence around the site before the equipment arrives.
examples.analytical: The sculptor's figure stands erect, a posture that Greek art associated with dignity and self-command.

nuance.analogy: Like a flagpole fixed straight up in a windless yard.
nuance.etymology: From Latin erigere, 'to raise up,' from e- 'out' and regere 'to guide.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'ee-REKT' or 'eh-RECT' with the wrong stress.
Using 'erect' as a casual synonym for 'stiff' or 'hard' in everyday contexts.

erect.etymology: From Middle English *erect*, a borrowing from Latin *ērectus* (“upright”), past participle of *ērigō* (“raise, set up”), from *ē-* (“out”) + *regō* (“to direct, keep straight, guide”).

senses.definition: A winged figure of a child representing love or its power.
senses.example: The sculptor carved a winged eros holding a bow, playfully aiming at the viewers.

senses.definition: Physical love; sexual desire.
A type of love that seeks fulfillment without violation or something else.
senses.example: Their marriage was built on eros, a passionate longing that sought fulfillment rather than mere duty.

senses.definition: Libido.
senses.example: Freud argued that eros drives much of human behavior, from creativity to desire.

senses.definition: Collective instincts for self-preservation; life drive.
senses.example: Freud's theory of eros described the instincts that keep individuals and species alive.

core.definition: In Greek thought and Christian theology, passionate love that desires union with what it finds beautiful or good, including romantic or sexual love.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable: AIR-ahs, with an American 'r' and an 'ah' in the second syllable. Don't say 'EE-ros' or 'ay-ROSE'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive in philosophy; in everyday American use, it suggests sexual desire and can sound clinical or suggestive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans meet 'eros' in philosophy, classics and theology, usually in contrast with agape. Outside those fields it sounds highbrow. The related adjective 'erotic' is common but has sexual connotations that 'eros' often does not.

distinctions.note: Agape is self-giving, unconditional love; eros desires and seeks what it finds valuable.
Philia is friendship or companionship; eros is passionate longing.
Lust is mainly sexual craving with a negative moral tone; eros can include longing for beauty, truth, or the good.

examples.everyday: In my philosophy class we talked about eros as the kind of love that wants to be close to what it admires.
examples.professional: The lecture contrasts eros and agape as two ways Christian writers describe human love.
examples.analytical: For Plato, eros is a longing that can ascend from physical beauty to the contemplation of the Good.

nuance.analogy: Like thirst: it reaches toward what it lacks, while agape is like a spring that gives freely.
nuance.etymology: From Greek erōs, 'love, desire,' also the name of the Greek god of love.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'EE-ros' or 'ee-ROSE'.
Treating eros and agape as identical.
Assuming eros is always sinful in Christian thought.
nuance.biblical_note: The noun eros does not appear in the Greek New Testament, which uses agape and philia. The Song of Solomon, in the RSV, celebrates romantic love between a man and a woman, and many Christian writers read it as affirming the goodness of erotic love within God's design.

senses.definition: To make a mistake.
senses.example: He erred in his calculations, and made many mistakes.

senses.definition: To sin.
senses.example: To err is human, to forgive, divine.

senses.definition: Elongated form of er (“sound of hesitation”).
senses.example: Err... what did you just say?

core.definition: To make a mistake, especially in judgment or behavior; to be wrong about something.

pronunciation.tip: This is an r-colored vowel like the one in 'fur' or 'bird', with no 'air' sound. It is a single sound, not two syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative; it usually means an honest mistake, not a moral failing, unless a religious or moral context is clear.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use err in casual speech; they say 'make a mistake' or 'get it wrong.' You will hear 'err on the side of caution' in news and advice, and 'to err is human' as a common saying. The interjection form, a drawn-out 'er,' is not standard; Americans say 'uh' or 'um' when hesitating.

distinctions.note: Make a mistake is everyday and neutral, while err is more formal and often appears in set phrases like err on the side of caution.
Sin is a moral or religious term for wrongdoing against God or ethics, while err means to go wrong in judgment or fact, though it can have moral overtones in religious writing.

collocations: err on the side of caution

examples.everyday: I think I erred by reading the directions too quickly, so let's start over.
examples.professional: We erred by approving the budget without checking the vendor's numbers, so we will review the process.
examples.analytical: The critic argues that the court erred when it treated the statute's ambiguous wording as clear.

nuance.analogy: To err is like taking a wrong turn while driving: you didn't mean to, but you're off the route until you correct course.
nuance.etymology: From Latin errare, meaning to wander or stray.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like 'air' (ER) instead of the r-colored vowel 'ur'.
Confusing err with error: 'I made an error' is more natural than 'I erred an error'.
Using err in casual speech where 'make a mistake' sounds more natural.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Bible, the idea of erring appears in the New Testament as planaō, meaning to lead astray or wander. In Matthew 22:29 Jesus tells the Sadducees that they are wrong because they do not know the Scriptures or the power of God, and Mark 12:24 gives a similar account. These passages show that error is tied to failing to know God's word and power.
patterns: err on the side of sth

err.etymology: From Middle English *erren*, from Old French *errer* (“to wander, err, mistake”), from Latin *errō* (“wander, stray, err, mistake”), from Proto-Indo-European **h₁ers-* (“to be angry, lose one's temper”).

senses.definition: Involving or relating to escalation.
senses.example: Officials worried that the latest airstrikes would trigger further escalatory responses from both sides.

core.definition: Tending to increase, intensify, or enlarge a conflict or situation step by step.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on ES, with a secondary stress on tor. The final ory is pronounced ree, not ory as in story or ory with a long o.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes an action that makes a conflict or situation more intense, often with a warning tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use escalatory mostly in political, military, and academic discussions about conflicts, sanctions, or disputes. In everyday talk, people use escalating or getting worse. The word is less common than escalating and sounds formal, so use it when you want to describe a quality of an action rather than an ongoing process.

distinctions.note: Escalatory describes a quality of an action that tends to intensify conflict, while escalating describes an ongoing process of growth or intensity.

examples.everyday: Let's not make this argument escalatory; we can talk calmly about the dishes.
examples.professional: The sanctions were criticized as escalatory, since each round was harsher than the last.
examples.analytical: Escalatory dynamics in arms races are self-reinforcing, because each side's response justifies the next.

nuance.analogy: An escalatory action is like a dial turned one notch higher each time, with no pressure to turn it back down.
nuance.etymology: From escalate, from escalade, a scaling ladder, from Latin scala, meaning ladder.
common_mistakes: Using escalatory in casual conversation, where escalating is more natural.
Pronouncing the final ory as ory; it is ree.
Confusing escalatory with escalator, the moving staircase; the two words have different meanings.

senses.definition: Existence without end, infinite time.
Existence outside of time.
A period of time which extends infinitely far into the future.
senses.example: Her grandmother spoke about eternity as a time that would never come to an end.

senses.definition: The remainder of time that elapses after death.
senses.example: The priest's sermon promised that the faithful would find peace in eternity.

senses.definition: A comparatively long time.
senses.example: It's been an eternity since we last saw each other.

core.definition: Existence without end, or the endless time that lies beyond history; in religion, life beyond time with God.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, 'TUR,' and reduce the middle syllable to 'nuh.' Do not say 'ET-er-nih-tee' with the stress on the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It can be solemn in religious contexts and hyperbolic in casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use eternity in religious contexts, poetry, speeches and sometimes in everyday exaggeration, such as 'it took an eternity.' In casual speech, people more often say 'forever' or 'ages.' The phrase 'for eternity' sounds formal or dramatic in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: Forever is an everyday word for a long or unending time, while eternity is more formal and often has religious or philosophical meaning.
Infinity is a mathematical concept about unbounded quantity, while eternity is about endless time or timeless existence.

examples.everyday: The line at the DMV took an eternity, and I still forgot my form.
examples.professional: The migration job has been running for an eternity, so I'm checking whether it's stuck.
examples.analytical: For Augustine, God's eternity is not endless time but the complete possession of life in one present moment.

nuance.analogy: Like a sea with no shore: you can sail for as long as you like and never reach an edge.
nuance.etymology: From Latin aeternitas, from aeternus, 'everlasting.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as 'ET-er-nih-tee.'
Using 'in eternity' in everyday speech where 'forever' is more natural.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word olam means a long or hidden duration, often translated as eternity or forever, while the Greek aiōn means an age and aiōnios describes what belongs to that age. Isaiah 57:15 describes God as the high and lofty One who inhabits eternity. Ecclesiastes 3:11 says God has set eternity in the human heart, meaning a sense of something beyond the visible life.

eternity.etymology: From Middle English *eternyte*, from Old French *eternité*, from Latin *aeternitās*.

senses.definition: Continuously, constantly, all the time (for the complete duration).
senses.example: People struggled to cope with the ever-increasing cost of living.

senses.definition: At any time.
senses.example: We've only ever talked on the phone.

senses.definition: As intensifier following an interrogative word.
senses.example: Was I ever glad to see you!

senses.definition: Indicates experiential aspect, once; has or have (done something) before.
senses.example: Have you ever tried making sourdough bread at home before?

senses.definition: Occurring at any time, occurring even but once during a timespan.
senses.example: The only ever example of this rare fossil was found in 1931.

senses.definition: Shortening of every.
senses.example: Ever kid in the class got a ribbon.

core.definition: At any time at all; used in questions and negative sentences to mean 'at any point' in someone's life or history.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and pronounce the final 'r' clearly because American English is rhotic. The second syllable is a weak schwa, so avoid saying 'EH-vur' with a strong vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, with no emotional charge in itself.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'ever' in questions like 'Have you ever tried sushi?' and with negatives like 'I haven't ever seen snow here.' In casual speech it is also used as an intensifier, as in 'What ever happened to him?' A natural reply to 'Have you ever been to Texas?' is 'Yes, once' or 'No, never.'

distinctions.note: 'Always' means every time or without exception, while 'ever' asks or states whether something happens at any time at all.
'Never' is a negative meaning 'at no time,' while 'ever' appears in questions and negatives like 'not ever,' which sounds informal.

examples.everyday: Have you ever tried the tacos at that place on Fifth Street?
examples.professional: Has the team ever measured the model's latency under peak load?
examples.analytical: Can any moral theory ever fully justify punishment without appealing to desert or consequence?

nuance.analogy: Like a camera searching an entire archive for one photo, 'ever' scans the whole timeline for any moment.
nuance.etymology: From Old English 'æfre,' meaning 'always, at any time.'
common_mistakes: Using 'ever' in a plain affirmative sentence where 'always' or 'once' fits better, such as 'I ever go there' instead of 'I always go there.'
Confusing 'ever' with 'every' in speech, since the two words sound similar in fast talk.

ever.etymology: From Middle English *ever*, from Old English *ǣfre*, originally a phrase whose first element undoubtedly consists of + *in* (“in”) + an element possibly from *feorh* (“life, existence”) (dative *fēore*).

senses.definition: Bearing several crops of fruit throughout the season.

core.definition: Producing fruit several times during a growing season, not just once. Said mostly of strawberries and some raspberries.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, with a weaker secondary stress on 'bear.' The first two syllables are rhotic, so say 'EV-er' with a clear r before 'bair-ing.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral, used in gardening and farming to describe plant behavior.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'everbearing' mainly in gardening catalogs, farm stands, and conversations about strawberries or raspberries. It is practical rather than emotional. A natural reply to 'Which strawberries should I plant?' might be 'Try an everbearing variety so you get fruit all summer.'

distinctions.note: 'June-bearing' strawberries produce one large crop in early summer, while 'everbearing' varieties produce smaller crops over several flushes.
'Perennial' means a plant lives for several years, while 'everbearing' describes how often it produces fruit during one season.

examples.everyday: We planted everbearing strawberries, so we've been picking a few every week since June.
examples.professional: The farm's everbearing berries give us a steadier harvest, which helps with weekly sales planning.
examples.analytical: Agronomists classify berry cultivars by fruiting pattern, and the everbearing habit trades a single large yield for repeated smaller ones.

nuance.analogy: Like a faucet that keeps dripping through the season instead of one big gush, the plant gives fruit in small, repeated batches.
nuance.etymology: Compound of 'ever' (from Old English 'æfre') and 'bearing,' from Old English 'beran' meaning 'to carry, bring forth.'
common_mistakes: Using 'everbearing' for plants that bear fruit every year; it refers to several crops within one season.
Spelling it as two words, 'ever bearing,' which is not standard in American gardening terms.

senses.definition: A female lamb.
A poor person's sole possession (in reference to the Bible, 2 Samuel xii).
senses.example: The widow clung to her one cow as if it were her ewe lamb, her only treasure.

core.definition: A young female sheep; figuratively, someone's single cherished possession, the one thing they love and will not give up.

pronunciation.tip: Ewe sounds exactly like 'you', and lamb has a silent b, so say 'lam'. Stress falls on EWE, with lamb lighter.

nuance.connotation: Positive or sentimental; it suggests tenderness and deep attachment, sometimes with the sense of a precious thing one is reluctant to lose.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use the phrase mainly when referring to the Bible or in literary and sentimental speech. In everyday talk they more often say apple of my eye or my baby for something cherished. The figurative sense works best when someone is protective of something they value.

distinctions.note: An ewe is any adult female sheep, while ewe lamb specifically means a young female before she has had lambs of her own.
Apple of my eye is a common informal expression for a person someone adores; ewe lamb is more literary and often refers to a single valued possession.
A pet is an animal kept for affection; ewe lamb is figurative and can refer to a possession or person treasured as unique.

collocations: the ewe lamb of the family

examples.everyday: Grandpa's old Mustang is his ewe lamb; nobody else is allowed to drive it.
examples.professional: The legacy billing system is our ewe lamb: everyone wants to change it, but nobody wants to risk breaking it.
examples.analytical: In Nathan's parable the poor man's ewe lamb stands for everything he owns, and David's anger shows how the story exposes his own sin.

nuance.analogy: A ewe lamb is like a family heirloom you would never sell, even at a high price.
nuance.etymology: Ewe comes from Old English ēowu and lamb from Old English lamb; the figurative sense comes from the Bible.
common_mistakes: Confusing ewe with you or yew (a tree), which sound the same.
Pronouncing the b in lamb, which is silent.
nuance.biblical_note: In 2 Samuel 12:1-4 the prophet Nathan tells King David a parable about a rich man who takes a poor man's one ewe lamb, a female lamb the poor man raised like a child, to feed a visitor. The Hebrew word behind the image is kivsah, a female lamb. In 2 Samuel 12:7-9 Nathan applies the story to David, who had taken Bathsheba and arranged Uriah's death, showing that the parable exposed David's own sin.

senses.definition: Attention to small details; accuracy.

core.definition: Careful, precise attention to detail; complete accuracy in measurement, description or behavior.

pronunciation.tip: Stress ZAK, the first syllable. The final -tude is pronounced tood, not tyood, and the middle syllable is short and reduced.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises careful, dependable precision.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use exactitude in formal writing, reviews and history, usually to describe careful work, a memory or a description. In daily conversation they say accuracy, precision, or be careful about details. Exactitude can sound pompous in casual talk, so keep it for emphasis or written prose.

distinctions.note: Accuracy is the common everyday word for correctness, while exactitude is more formal and emphasizes meticulous care.
Precision emphasizes fine measurement and narrow limits, often in technical contexts; exactitude emphasizes care in matching facts.

examples.everyday: He follows the recipe with real exactitude, down to the gram.
examples.professional: The auditor checked every invoice with exactitude before signing the report.
examples.analytical: Medieval theologians pursued doctrinal exactitude, defining terms carefully to block misreadings.

nuance.analogy: Like a jeweler's scale that registers a single gram: the exactitude is the fineness of the instrument.
nuance.etymology: From Latin exactitudo, from exactus, exact.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the ending as tyood instead of tood.
Using exactitude in everyday chat where accuracy sounds more natural.

exactitude.etymology: From French *exactitude*, from *exact*, from Latin *exactus*, perfect passive participle of *exigō* (“demand, claim as due" or "measure by a standard, weigh, test”), from *ex* (“out”) + *agō* (“drive”).

senses.definition: In an exasperating manner; frustratingly.
senses.example: The printer jammed exasperatingly often, so we spent the morning clearing paper and restarting it.

core.definition: In a way that is extremely irritating or frustrating, to the point of exhausting someone's patience.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable of the stem, ZAS, and keep the middle syllables light. The ending -ly is a quick 'lee', and the -ing sound is nasal, with no separate 'ee' before the -ly.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It emphasizes how irritating something is, often with a note of humor.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use exasperatingly to intensify an adjective in everyday complaints: 'The line was exasperatingly slow.' It is more emotional than 'frustratingly' and often appears in reviews, work discussions and casual complaints. In a formal argument, it can show frustration with the reasoning. A natural reply is 'Tell me about it.'

distinctions.note: Annoyingly is lighter and more casual; exasperatingly implies the situation pushes someone to the edge of patience.
Frustratingly is very close; use it when a goal is blocked, and exasperatingly when repeated irritation builds up.

examples.everyday: The Wi-Fi keeps dropping, and it's exasperatingly slow in the evenings.
examples.professional: The build keeps failing on a dependency that is exasperatingly hard to reproduce on a local machine.
examples.analytical: The argument is exasperatingly circular: it assumes the conclusion it is supposed to prove.

nuance.analogy: Like a song stuck in your head that you can't turn off, wearing you down with every repeat.
nuance.etymology: From exasperating, from Latin exasperare, 'to make rough, irritate', plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Placing the stress on the final syllable of the stem rather than on ZAS.
Using 'exasperatingly' to describe a person's feelings; the feeling is 'exasperated', and the cause is 'exasperating'.

senses.definition: Resembling an exclamation.
Emphatic.
senses.example: Her exclamatory reply, Absolutely not!, made everyone at the table turn and stare.

core.definition: Expressing strong emotion, such as surprise or excitement, often with exclamation points or loud, expressive speech.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, KLAM, not the last syllable. The first vowel is a short i sound, not eks or eh, and the final -ry is a light ee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when describing expressive language; mildly negative if it suggests overwrought emotion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly use exclamatory in grammar and writing, as in an exclamatory sentence that ends with an exclamation point. In speech, people more often say excited, emphatic or enthusiastic. Calling a person exclamatory sounds formal or critical, as if they talk too loudly.

distinctions.note: Emphatic describes a strong, firm statement; exclamatory describes a statement that is expressive in tone or punctuation.
Effusive means showing warm, excessive praise or emotion; exclamatory is simply expressed with an exclamation.

examples.everyday: Her text was exclamatory: 'We got the house!!!' and she added three emojis.
examples.professional: The sales email was exclamatory, with three exclamation points and the word huge in every line.
examples.analytical: The sentence is exclamatory in form but interrogative in function, asking the reader to reconsider what seems obvious.

nuance.analogy: Like a shout written on paper: the exclamation point is the raised voice on the page.
nuance.etymology: From exclamation (from Latin exclamare, to cry out) plus the adjective suffix -ory, meaning of or like.
common_mistakes: Using exclamatory to mean loud in a person's voice; say loud or emphatic instead.
Stressing the last syllable, as in ik-sklam-uh-TOR-ee; the stress belongs on the second syllable.

senses.definition: Having the capacity to be expanded.
senses.example: an expandable baton

senses.definition: Anything that can be expanded.
senses.example: Mobile homes include doublewides, expandables, and single units.

core.definition: Able to be made larger, extended or enlarged, such as a computer system, storage device or folding table.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SPAN, and the final -able is a weak, reduced syllable that sounds like bul. Avoid saying the a in the middle as a strong vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral; it suggests flexibility and room to grow.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use expandable often in shopping, technology and home contexts, such as expandable storage or an expandable table. It is common in product descriptions and everyday conversation. Do not confuse it with expendable, which means something that can be given up or sacrificed.

distinctions.note: Expandable is the common everyday word, while expansible is rare and mostly appears in older or formal writing.
Extendable is also common, but it usually means something that can be lengthened, while expandable usually means something that can grow in size or capacity.

examples.everyday: We bought an expandable dining table, so we can seat eight people when the whole family visits.
examples.professional: Our storage plan is expandable, so we can add capacity without migrating the data.
examples.analytical: The theory treats the state as expandable in principle, though real institutions resist such growth.

nuance.analogy: An expandable table is like an accordion: it stays compact until you need more room, then opens up.
nuance.etymology: From expand, from Latin expandere meaning to spread out, plus -able.
common_mistakes: Confusing expandable with expendable, which means something that can be sacrificed or easily discarded.
Pronouncing the middle syllable as ex-PAN-dah-bul rather than ik-SPAN-duh-bul.

senses.definition: Any of a class of continuous probability distributions used to model the time between events that occur independently at a constant average rate.

core.definition: A continuous probability distribution that models the waiting time between independent events that happen at a constant average rate.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on NEN in exponential and on BYOO in distribution. The 'ex' is an unstressed schwa, not 'ox,' and the 'tri' in distribution reduces to 'truh.' In American English the -tion ending is pronounced 'shun.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It has no emotional tone and is used only in mathematics, statistics, and data science.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use exponential distribution in statistics courses, data science work, reliability engineering, and queueing theory. Outside technical settings, people rarely use it. In conversation with coworkers, they often shorten it to 'exponential' when the context is clear.

distinctions.note: A normal distribution is symmetric and bell-shaped, describing many natural measurements. An exponential distribution is skewed and models waiting times, with most values near zero.
A Poisson distribution counts how many events happen in a fixed interval. An exponential distribution measures the time between those events.

collocations: the rate parameter of an exponential distribution
the memoryless property of the exponential distribution

examples.everyday: Our support center says the wait times follow an exponential distribution, so long waits are rare but do happen.
examples.professional: We model the time between server failures with an exponential distribution, which assumes a constant failure rate.
examples.analytical: The exponential distribution is the only continuous distribution with the memoryless property.

nuance.analogy: Think of waiting for a bus that arrives at random, on average every ten minutes: the chance it comes in the next minute is the same at any moment, and long waits become less and less likely.
nuance.etymology: Exponential comes from Latin exponere 'set forth,' via exponent; distribution comes from Latin distribuere 'divide up.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'eks-po-NEN-shul' with a full 'ox' vowel in the first syllable; it should be a reduced schwa.
Confusing it with exponential growth, which describes a quantity increasing over time rather than a probability model.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to extension.
Having great extent.
senses.example: The empire's extensional reach spanned three continents by the close of the century.

core.definition: In logic, relating to a term's extension, meaning the set of things it refers to, rather than its intension or definition.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on SHUH, the third syllable, with a lighter secondary stress on STEN. Many learners stress the first syllable or pronounce the ending as 'shun-al' with two full syllables instead of a reduced schwa.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical, used precisely in logic, philosophy, and semantics.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word almost only in logic, philosophy of language, and computer science, where it is paired with 'intensional.' In ordinary conversation nobody says it. If you need a casual word, say 'the actual things it refers to' or 'what it actually picks out.'

distinctions.note: Intensional refers to meaning or definition, while extensional refers to the actual objects or set the term picks out.
Extensive means large in scope or amount, while extensional is a specialized term about reference in logic.

examples.everyday: When we say 'bird,' I mean the actual animals, which is the extensional meaning, not the idea of a bird.
examples.professional: In the database, the extensional view treats a table as the set of rows it currently contains.
examples.analytical: An extensional semantics assigns truth conditions by identifying the objects each predicate actually applies to.

nuance.analogy: If a term is a net, its intension is the rule for what the net catches, and its extension is the actual fish inside it.
nuance.etymology: Formed from extension, from Latin extensio, a stretching out.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'extensive,' which describes size or scope.
Stressing the first syllable instead of the third.

senses.definition: The principle that objects are equal if and only if their observed properties are the same, regardless of internal processes that lead to those properties.
senses.example: Our philosophy seminar debated whether extensionality should govern how we judge two objects identical.

senses.definition: The principle that functions are equal if and only if they operate on the same domain and for any given element of the domain the result of each of the functions is the same.
senses.example: Under extensionality, two functions that always return the same outputs for the same inputs are considered equal.

senses.definition: The principle, codified in the axiom of extensionality, that sets are equal if and only if they contain the same elements.
senses.example: Set theory begins with extensionality, which says two sets are equal exactly when they share the same members.

core.definition: In logic and mathematics, the principle that two things are equal when they have the same members or the same observable behavior, regardless of how they were built.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on NAL, the fourth syllable, shifting from the stress on STEN in extension. The t in the final -ity is flapped and sounds closer to a quick d, so say it as tee in quick speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use extensionality almost only in logic, set theory, type theory, programming language theory, philosophy of language, and some artificial intelligence and knowledge representation work. In everyday conversation it is rare, and people would say it depends on what things are made of, not on how they were produced. In a technical setting, pair it with its opposite, intensionality, to make your meaning clear.

distinctions.note: Extensionality judges identity by the actual members or outputs, while intensionality judges it by the meaning or definition that picks out those members.
Extension is the set of things a term applies to, while extensionality is the principle that equal extensions make things identical.

examples.everyday: My roommate is a math major, and she keeps saying extensionality means two things are the same if they have the same members.
examples.professional: Our knowledge graph relies on extensionality, so two entities with identical attributes are merged into one record.
examples.analytical: Extensionality holds that a set is determined entirely by its members, so two sets with exactly the same members are identical.

nuance.analogy: Like judging two recipes by the dishes they produce, not by the cooking method, since identical dishes count as the same.
nuance.etymology: From extension, from Latin extensio 'a stretching out', with the suffix -ality forming the abstract noun.
common_mistakes: Confusing extensionality with extension, which is the set of things a term applies to.
Placing the stress on the STEN syllable instead of NAL, as in extension.

senses.definition: That attenuates or lessens the seriousness of something, e.g. by providing a mitigating excuse for it.
senses.example: The judge considered the extenuating circumstances, including the defendant's recent job loss, before sentencing him.

core.definition: Making a wrongdoing or failure seem less serious, usually because of circumstances that partly excuse it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress STEN, the second syllable. Pronounce 'yoo' as in 'you,' and 'ay' as in 'day.' The ending '-ing' is short, with no 'ing' vowel stretched out.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly formal. It describes reasons that reduce blame, and it is usually said sympathetically.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use 'extenuating circumstances' in school, work, legal, and news contexts, such as a missed exam or late payment. In casual talk people say 'with a good reason' or 'because of something unavoidable.' It sounds a bit formal, so it works well in emails and official forms.

distinctions.note: Mitigating is the more common legal term in American courts, while extenuating is used more in everyday formal writing.
Excusable describes a thing that can be forgiven, while extenuating describes the reasons or circumstances that make it less blameworthy.

examples.everyday: My teacher gave me another day because of extenuating circumstances, since my mom was in the hospital.
examples.professional: Please note any extenuating circumstances, such as a family emergency, on the absence request form.
examples.analytical: The chaplain weighed the extenuating factors, but he still judged the act to be sinful.

nuance.analogy: Extenuating circumstances are like a rainstorm that makes you late: you still arrived late, but people understand why.
nuance.etymology: From extenuate, from Latin extenuare, to make thin.
common_mistakes: Using 'extenuating' as a verb; the verb is 'extenuate,' and the adjective is 'extenuating.'
Pronouncing the middle syllable as 'wah-tuh,' instead of 'yoo-ay.'

extenuating.etymology: From Latin *ex* (“to delete, to cross out”) and *tenuatus*, past participle of *tenuare* (“to make thin”) + Middle English *-ing*.

senses.definition: Of feelings, a person's spirit, a state of affairs, etc.: put out, as if like a fire; quenched, suppressed.
senses.example: His hope was extinct after the third rejection letter arrived.

senses.definition: Of customs, ideas, laws and legal rights, offices, organizations, languages, etc.: no longer existing or in use; defunct, discontinued, obsolete; specifically, of a title of nobility: no longer having any person qualified to hold it.
senses.example: Luckily, such ideas about race are extinct in current sociological theory.

senses.definition: Of an animal or plant species or group of species, a group of people, a family, etc. having no living members, representatives, or descendants. (Discuss this sense)
senses.example: Dinosaurs have been extinct for millions of years.

senses.definition: Of a geological feature: no longer active; specifically, of a volcano: no longer erupting.
senses.example: Most of the volcanos on this island are now extinct.

senses.definition: Of a radioisotope: no longer occurring primordially due to having decayed away completely, because it has a relatively short half-life.
senses.example: Technetium is extinct on Earth, having decayed completely since the planet formed.

senses.definition: Synonym of extinguish.
senses.example: He extincted the lantern and waited in the dark for the patrol to pass.

senses.definition: To cause (an animal or plant species) to die out completely or become extinct (adjective etymology 1 sense 2.3).
senses.example: Hunting and habitat loss extinct the passenger pigeon within a few decades.

senses.definition: Synonym of extinction (“the action of becoming or making extinct; annihilation”).
senses.example: Ecologists fear the extinct of the frog will follow the collapse of its wetland.
